title: Saudi Arabia intercepts Houthi missile as Trump threatens new strikes
full_text:
Gold set for steepest weekly drop in over four months as prices fall below $4,000
Investing.com -- Saudi Arabia intercepted a Houthi ballistic missile targeting Riyadh on Saturday as renewed U.S. threats against Iran and escalating regional attacks intensified fears of a broader Middle East conflict.
The Saudi-led coalition said its air defences destroyed the missile following emergency warnings in Riyadh, Najran and Wadi al-Dawasir. Authorities subsequently declared the danger over.
The coalition also reported intercepting a drone over Saudi Arabia’s Eastern Province, while Houthi-affiliated media reported fresh air strikes in Yemen’s Saada governorate.
The developments followed President Donald Trump’s warning that Washington could launch another military campaign against Iran, invoking Operation Epic Fury, which began in February.
U.S. Ambassador to Turkiye Tom Barrack separately suggested strikes could occur as early as this weekend, although Trump later said he knew nothing about such plans.
Energy markets have reacted sharply to the escalating threats. Brent crude reached $117.30 a barrel on Friday, while West Texas Intermediate climbed to $103, amid concerns over supply disruptions.
October has also become the deadliest month for commercial shipping security in the Strait of Hormuz by number of confirmed attacks, with at least 28 vessel strikes recorded, according to Washington Institute data reported by Reuters.
The institute counted 113 attacks since February, while the International Maritime Organization recorded 120 incidents.
Meanwhile, U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz said Washington could maintain its naval blockade of Iran for the foreseeable future.
Diplomatic efforts continue despite the military threats. International Atomic Energy Agency chief Rafael Grossi said the agency was technically prepared to resume nuclear verification in Iran, emphasising the need for a negotiated agreement.
Iran’s deputy UN envoy maintained that Tehran had not abandoned its nuclear safeguards obligations, citing security concerns over inspectors returning.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian is expected to meet Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow next week during a gas exporters’ summit.
Separately, Israel imposed sweeping restrictions across the occupied West Bank following a shooting that killed two Israeli soldiers near Hebron. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu threatened an extensive military operation, while Israeli forces conducted raids and demolitions.

title: Marco Rubio calls on those seeking change in Cuba to partner with CIA
full_text:
Gold set for steepest weekly drop in over four months as prices fall below $4,000
By Bo Erickson and Kanishka Singh
FORT MYERS, Florida, Oct 23 (Reuters) - US Secretary of State Marco Rubio called on those seeking change in Cuba to partner with the CIA as President Donald Trump said Washington would "take care of Cuba" after dealing with Iran and send in the top US diplomat to finish the deal.
DETAILS AND QUOTES:
• "We’ll take care of Cuba on our way back from Iran ... then we’re going to send Marco Rubio in to finish up the deal," Trump told a rally in Florida.
• "To those who seek to create positive change in Cuba - now is the time," Rubio, who has been handling much of the Cuba-related policy for Trump, said on X on Friday.
• Rubio urged those disappointed by Cuba’s government to "seize this opportunity to create the change you desire through a discrete partnership with the CIA," without elaborating further.
• The Trump administration has previously stated its goal is to change Cuba’s communist government.
• A US-imposed oil blockade implemented earlier this year has put Cuba under severe strain as it contends with fuel shortages and blackouts exacerbated by failing infrastructure.
• Washington has maintained an embargo on Cuba for over 60 years.
• The Trump administration has been stepping up pressure on Havana after the US military in January seized then-Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro in a deadly raid.
• Cuba’s foreign minister told the UN General Assembly last month Cuba would always be open for dialogue with Washington.
• UN rights experts have condemned the oil blockade as a violation of international law while rights advocates say the Trump administration’s threats have echoed an imperialist approach.
• Trump predicted last month the US and Cuba would reach an agreement and that he did not think military action would be necessary.

title: Amazon’s AWS cloud capacity largely sold out through 2027, CEO says
full_text:
Gold set for steepest weekly drop in over four months as prices fall below $4,000
Investing.com -- Amazon (NASDAQ: AMZN) CEO Andy Jassy said Friday that the company’s cloud computing capacity is largely sold out through 2027, with substantial commitments extending into 2028 as demand for artificial intelligence infrastructure continues to surge.
Speaking during a video podcast with Andreessen Horowitz co-founder Ben Horowitz and general partner Erik Torenberg, Jassy said Amazon Web Services (AWS) is struggling to expand infrastructure quickly enough to meet demand.
AI developers and enterprise customers are increasingly seeking computing resources to train, deploy and operate artificial intelligence models, placing significant pressure on available capacity.
The supply constraints come despite Amazon’s plans to spend approximately $220 billion on capital expenditure during 2026, reflecting its aggressive investment in data centres and supporting infrastructure.
Jassy suggested that additional spending could be justified given the scale of demand, noting that the company’s available cloud capacity for 2026 has already been fully committed.
Most of the large capacity allocations for 2027 have also been reserved, while a significant portion of 2028 capacity is already accounted for.
However, AWS continues to retain some computing resources for customers using its on-demand services, including Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (EC2) and Amazon Bedrock.
EC2 provides scalable cloud servers for businesses running applications and workloads, while Bedrock enables developers to access artificial intelligence models and build generative AI applications.
The distinction allows AWS to maintain access for customers requiring flexible computing resources despite the substantial long-term infrastructure commitments.
The comments highlight the growing importance of securing cloud capacity as technology companies compete to expand their AI capabilities.
They also underscore the capital-intensive nature of the AI infrastructure expansion, with major cloud providers committing substantial resources ahead of anticipated customer demand.
Amazon is scheduled to report its third-quarter financial results on October 29, when investors will be watching for further details on AWS growth, infrastructure spending and capacity expansion.

title: US Justice Dept sues to block possible Alaska election of Democrat to Senate
full_text:
By Jan Wolfe
Oct 23 (Reuters) - The Trump administration has sued Alaska to preemptively block the state from certifying the results of its US Senate race if the Republican incumbent candidate loses narrowly, saying voters could be confused because two Republicans on the ballot have almost identical names.
The Department of Justice’s lawsuit, filed in federal court in Anchorage on Thursday, signals the willingness of President Donald Trump’s administration to contest the results of the November 3 midterm elections that will decide control of the US Congress, where his fellow Republicans narrowly control both chambers.
The administration has taken an increasingly aggressive approach to election oversight, pressing states for voter-registration data and arguing that stricter measures are needed to ensure public confidence in the vote. Critics, including Democratic and some Republican election officials, view the moves as federal overreach.
Control of the Senate could come down to Alaska, where incumbent Republican Dan S. Sullivan is running a close race against Democrat Mary Peltola.
The suit, which names the state and local election officials as defendants, takes issue with the presence of another contender in the race, another Republican named Dan J. Sullivan Jr, alleging he is running "with the intention of misleading supporters of Senator Sullivan into voting for him."
The DOJ asks a judge to block the certification of an outcome "that may be impacted by voter confusion," so that there can be "an investigation to determine whether votes cast for Daniel J. Sullivan were meant to be cast for Senator Sullivan."
Trump told reporters on Friday that he supported the lawsuit, saying "I’m the one that said do it."
A DOJ spokesperson said in a statement that the agency is taking "necessary steps to ensure that this frivolous candidacy does not undermine the integrity of Alaska’s election or the will of its voters.”
Election officials around the country have told Reuters they are preparing for potential federal interference in the elections, including legal challenges and disputes over voting that could disrupt certification of the results.
Trump has a long history of challenging election outcomes and encouraging supporters to contest results he views as unfavorable.
Alaska’s other US senator, Senator Lisa Murkowski from Trump’s Republican Party, said on Friday the Justice Department "should never have filed this lawsuit."
Election law experts said the lawsuit has no merit and seeks relief not allowed under federal law.
"In short, like many Department letters over the last few years, it is designed to win the press release rather than the litigation," wrote Notre Dame law professor Derek Muller in a blog post, adding that "the legal argument is one of the worst ones I’ve ever seen."
Trump’s administration "has absolutely no authority to tell Alaska when or how to certify the results of its Senate election," said David Becker of the Center for Election Innovation and Research, a nonpartisan group that advises election officials, adding that "this issue has already been fully litigated by Alaska’s courts."
The unelected Sullivan, a former US Forest Service worker and elementary school teacher, filed to run as a candidate on May 29, seeking to unseat Dan S. Sullivan and "put Alaska first," according to his campaign website, which advertised "Dan Sullivan Challenges Dan Sullivan for US Senate Seat."
Dan J. Sullivan has denied in interviews with US news outlets that his aim is to cause confusion or divert votes from Dan S. Sullivan.
The Alaska Supreme Court in June permitted the challenger Sullivan to appear on the ballot. He will appear without a party designation next to his name, while the senator will be listed as the Republican incumbent.
Peltola, the Democratic candidate, told MS NOW on Friday that because of how the candidates are displayed on the ballot "there just isn’t much room for confusion." The lawsuit is "sending a message that Dan Sullivan does not believe that Alaskans are sophisticated enough to know exactly who they’re voting for," she added.
Trump’s approval rating has fallen to a record low, hit by rising diesel and gasoline prices during the Iran war, which has proven deeply unpopular with voters.
Public opinion polls suggest Republicans may lose control of one or both chambers of Congress, which would likely limit Trump’s ability to enact some of his policy agenda in the final two years of his presidency.

title: Boeing 777 freighter output halted for two months over supplier row - Reuters
full_text:
Gold set for steepest weekly drop in over four months as prices fall below $4,000
Investing.com -- Boeing (NYSE) has suspended production of its 777 freighter for nearly two months following a dispute with a key parts supplier, Reuters reported Friday exclusively, citing company workers and court documents.
The disruption has also affected production of Boeing’s 767 aircraft, including commercial freighters and KC-46 aerial refuelling tankers used by the U.S. military.
The dispute centres on Florida-based supplier Vaero, which allegedly stopped delivering trailing-edge rib kits used in aircraft wing assembly.
According to an August legal complaint reviewed by Reuters, Boeing identified Vaero as the sole supplier of the critical component, describing the parts as essential to maintaining production.
The interruption was costing the aerospace manufacturer as much as $6.5 million daily, according to the complaint.
Although the companies settled in late September, production of the 777 freighter has not resumed, three Boeing workers familiar with the situation told Reuters.
Some components have since arrived for the 767 programme, allowing limited progress on affected aircraft.
Meanwhile, Boeing is reportedly working to bring manufacturing of the trailing-edge rib kits in-house to reduce its dependence on the supplier.
The disruption has forced the company to remove two partially assembled 777 freighters from its final assembly line in Everett, Washington.
One of those aircraft was identified through aviation consultancy IBA data as destined for FedEx (NYSE).
Boeing’s next-generation 777X programme has not been affected because it uses composite wings rather than the components involved in the dispute.
The company has delivered 21 777 freighters so far this year, according to its published delivery figures.
Several additional aircraft whose wings were assembled before the supply interruption could still be delivered before the end of 2026.
The production setback comes as Boeing faces continued pressure to stabilise manufacturing operations and maintain deliveries across its commercial and defence programmes.
Neither Boeing nor Vaero provided comments to Reuters, while FedEx also did not respond to requests for comment.

title: Investing.com’s stocks of the week
full_text:
Buy pullback in this chip stock, Mizuho says
Investing.com -- Cybersecurity names gained ground on a global software alert while Meta declined and a fresh escalation in the Middle East pushed crude to highs.
Here are Investing.com’s stocks of the week:
Cybersecurity stocks
Cybersecurity names were among the week's strong performers after an emergency security update for PHP, the programming language used by roughly 70% of websites worldwide, triggered a global alert.
Two critical vulnerabilities disclosed this week could allow hackers to take remote control of affected servers.
The incident highlights a growing challenge, with artificial intelligence accelerating the discovery of software weaknesses while potentially making them easier to exploit.
Okta led the moves with a 14% gain over the week, followed by Palo Alto Networks and CrowdStrike, both up 11%, and Cloudflare, up 9%.
Meta Platforms
Meta fell 7% on Thursday and is down 9.1% over the week after Wednesday’s post-close results, with a surprise plan to issue a new class of non-voting stock overshadowing stronger-than-expected third-quarter revenue.
The company’s special committee said in its filing that the move was motivated not only by keeping CEO Mark Zuckerberg in California but also by “an increasingly challenging environment for raising capital,” citing recent and anticipated raises at Alphabet, SpaceX, Anthropic and OpenAI to fund the same AI growth.
The committee added that while Meta has sufficient resources for current needs, it would be prudent to act before more companies absorb available capital in the market. The Class C shares are intended for equity offerings from time to time and could be available as early as the end of 2026.
Tesla and SpaceX
Tesla gained 4.6% over the week, and SpaceX added 0.6% after both reported results and confirmed they are examining a tie-up.
Tesla delivered better-than-expected third-quarter earnings, with free cash flow and capital expenditure coming in ahead of Wall Street estimates. SpaceX also topped expectations.
Each company has established an independent special committee to explore a potential merger, CEO Elon Musk said, emphasizing that while independent directors are actively evaluating the transaction, talks remain at an early stage with no guarantee of an agreement.
JPMorgan analysts said they see the potential structure as likely to be a SpaceX-led all-stock deal, adding that at current Tesla market capitalization levels, a 30% to 35% premium typical for such transactions “would imply a merger of equals and clear the threshold for Musk maintaining >50% voting control of the combined entity.”
Oil stocks
Energy names advanced as crude pushed to fresh highs, with Brent climbing above $117 and WTI above $103, with both up more than 3% on Friday.
SLB leads the group with a 6.7% weekly gain. The oilfield services company also reported results on Friday. Occidental Petroleum rose 3.4%, Chevron gained 3.2%, ConocoPhillips added 3.1% and Exxon Mobil was 1.8% higher.
Moderna
Moderna declined this week, tumbling more than 17% on Thursday, with Merck also falling, after what appeared to be an early release of closely watched trial results for the companies’ experimental cancer vaccine.
The data appeared on medical news website Oncology Central at around 12:30 p.m. ET before being taken down shortly afterward. The results had been scheduled for presentation at the ESMO Congress on Saturday.
Citi maintained its Sell rating and questioned whether the vaccine’s benefit justifies the complexity of individualized tumor harvesting and manufacturing.
Bernstein kept its Market Perform rating and described the move as a “sell the news event,” while BMO Capital Markets said the decline reflects the high expectations built into the stock’s large gains this year.
Mizuho analyst Jared Holz called Moderna a “do-not-trade” stock for many investors given the extreme volatility.

title: Russia, Ukraine agree to local ceasefire as new peace talks planned - Reuters
full_text:
Buy pullback in this chip stock, Mizuho says
Investing.com -- Russia and Ukraine have agreed to a temporary ceasefire in the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky to facilitate humanitarian operations, while negotiators prepare for another round of U.S.-mediated peace talks in November, Reuters reported Friday.
The ceasefire, scheduled to begin October 27, will allow humanitarian aid deliveries and civilian evacuations through designated safe corridors.
The agreement was coordinated with assistance from U.S. First Lady Melania Trump, who has also been involved in efforts to reunite Ukrainian children taken to Russia with their families.
Russian military chief Valery Gerasimov said troops would suspend operations from 4 a.m. local time on Tuesday.
Ukrainian officials said the humanitarian mission would include clearing mines from access roads, delivering essential supplies and evacuating vulnerable residents.
Oleshky, located across the Dnipro River from Ukrainian-controlled Kherson, has approximately 1,700 to 2,000 residents remaining, compared with 24,000 before the war.
Meanwhile, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said representatives from Ukraine, Russia and the United States were preparing technical-level peace negotiations during the first half of November.
Abu Dhabi is being considered as a venue, although a U.S. official indicated Switzerland remained another possibility.
Zelenskiy expressed hope that the discussions would eventually lead to a meeting between national leaders.
However, tensions between Washington and Kyiv persist over restrictions affecting Starlink communications used by Ukrainian forces.
President Donald Trump said he would contact SpaceX chief executive Elon Musk if necessary to resolve the issue.
Ukraine maintains that speed restrictions introduced on October 13 remain in place.
Any peace agreement would require substantial security guarantees and funding to sustain Ukraine’s military for another decade, Zelenskiy said.
Separately, Russia and Ukraine exchanged 270 prisoners of war each on Friday, marking their first such exchange since August.
Ukrainian prosecutors reported that more than 19,000 civilians, including 762 children, have been killed since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022.

title: U.S. repeatedly asked Musk to restrict or expand Starlink access, Reuters says
full_text:
Investing.com -- Successive U.S. administrations have asked Elon Musk’s SpaceX to alter Starlink access in several countries, Reuters reported Friday exclusively.
Citing six former senior U.S. officials, Reuters reported that both the Biden and Trump administrations sought changes to Starlink coverage to support allies and disrupt communications used by adversaries.
Under former President Joe Biden, officials requested restrictions on terminals allegedly used by Iran-backed groups, including Hezbollah in Lebanon and the Houthis in Yemen.
Intelligence shared with SpaceX indicated that militants had obtained Starlink equipment through intermediaries, prompting requests to identify and deactivate specific terminals.
At least some terminals were subsequently disabled, according to former officials familiar with the discussions.
Meanwhile, Washington sought expanded Starlink access in Ukraine following Russia’s 2022 invasion and in Iran during anti-government protests that year.
President Donald Trump’s administration reportedly pursued similar arrangements following U.S.-Israeli strikes against Iran in 2025 and 2026, although activation of the terminals has not been publicly confirmed.
The disclosures follow recent restrictions on Ukraine’s Starshield military satellite service, which Kyiv says have disrupted drone operations and battlefield communications.
Reuters previously reported that the order to reduce Starshield speeds originated inside the White House.
Musk has maintained that Starshield systems are controlled by the U.S. government, with operational restrictions ultimately determined by military authorities and the president.
Trump said Friday he would contact Musk if necessary to resolve Ukraine’s communications problems.
The controversy has intensified concerns among European officials about dependence on SpaceX infrastructure for critical military capabilities.
Ukraine currently lacks a comparable alternative to Starlink for frontline communications and drone operations.
Democratic lawmaker Jason Crow has also called for greater transparency over the restrictions, questioning the national security implications of relying heavily on private companies.
SpaceX did not respond to Reuters’ requests for comment.

title: UK to inject £20.4 billion into state-backed lenders in budget, FT reports
full_text:
Investing.com -- British Chancellor John Healey is expected to announce £20.4 billion ($27.3 billion) in additional funding for two state-backed financial institutions in Wednesday’s budget, the Financial Times reported, citing confirmation from the UK Treasury.
The funding will strengthen the National Wealth Fund and British Business Bank, supporting investment in strategic industries and infrastructure projects across the country.
According to the Treasury, the National Wealth Fund will receive an additional £15.4 billion ($20.6 billion), while the British Business Bank will receive a further £5 billion ($7 billion).
The capital injections will be distributed over approximately five years, providing additional financial resources to support businesses and investment projects.
The Treasury estimates the funding could help support around 100,000 jobs by 2035, particularly in artificial intelligence, defence and green energy.
A Treasury spokesperson said the additional capital would help British businesses expand while directing investment towards industries, infrastructure and regions capable of generating employment and long-term economic growth.
The Financial Times first reported the planned funding increase, which the Treasury subsequently confirmed.
The announcement comes as Healey prepares his first budget under Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s government, with investors closely monitoring the administration’s approach to public borrowing and economic growth.
The planned capital boost highlights the government’s intention to support private-sector investment through existing state-backed financial institutions.
The National Wealth Fund focuses on financing projects that support Britain’s infrastructure and strategic economic priorities, while the British Business Bank helps improve access to finance for businesses.
The additional resources could expand both institutions’ capacity to support investment without relying exclusively on direct government spending programmes.
Wednesday’s budget will provide further details on how the funding fits into the government’s broader fiscal plans, including its approach to borrowing, taxation and economic development.

title: SpaceX’s $40bn AI debt deal faces hurdles amid credit market turmoil - Bloomberg
full_text:
Investing.com -- SpaceX’s proposed $40 billion AI financing deal has hit obstacles amid credit market volatility and rising borrowing costs, Bloomberg reported exclusively, citing people familiar with the matter.
The proposed transaction would finance purchases of Nvidia (NASDAQ) chips through a special purpose vehicle (SPV), allowing SpaceX to keep the borrowing off its balance sheet and protect its investment-grade credit ratings.
Goldman Sachs (NYSE) is leading discussions with investors headed by Apollo Global Management (NYSE), according to the report.
Apollo-backed Atlas SP is expected to manage the financing vehicle, while Pacific Investment Management Co. is also considering participating.
However, recent volatility in credit markets has complicated negotiations over borrowing costs as investors reassess the risks associated with financing large-scale AI infrastructure projects.
Earlier discussions placed yields on a subordinated portion of the debt around the mid-8% range, although worsening market conditions have prompted renewed pricing negotiations.
The proposed financing would involve three tranches of privately placed bonds, including a subordinated portion estimated at $25 billion to $30 billion.
Other tranches would total approximately $10 billion and up to $5 billion, according to Bloomberg.
The structure follows an earlier financing arrangement involving Elon Musk’s AI startup xAI that failed to achieve its intended accounting treatment.
SpaceX subsequently recognised approximately $13 billion in debt after auditors determined the arrangement did not qualify as a completed sale-leaseback transaction.
The latest financing discussions follow SpaceX’s third-quarter results, which showed its AI business turning profitable for the first time.
The company’s Memphis data centres have increasingly generated revenue by supplying computing capacity to external AI developers and major technology companies.
SpaceX executives have indicated that additional borrowing will be necessary to support expansion while maintaining investment-grade credit ratings.
The proposed deal also follows Apollo’s involvement in a major AI chip financing arrangement involving Anthropic and Broadcom (NASDAQ).

title: Windward Bio seeks Nasdaq listing to fund respiratory, skin disease drug trials
full_text:
Investing.com -- Windward Bio Group, a Swiss biotechnology company backed by Novo Holdings, has filed for an initial public offering in the U.S. to finance clinical trials of experimental treatments for respiratory and inflammatory diseases.
The Basel-based company submitted its registration documents to the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission on Friday, outlining plans to list on the Nasdaq Global Market under the ticker WWB.
Founded in 2024, Windward is developing antibody-based treatments targeting severe asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and inflammatory skin conditions.
Its drug pipeline includes a monoclonal antibody undergoing advanced clinical trials for respiratory diseases and a bispecific antibody in early-stage testing for inflammatory conditions, including eczema.
The company reported a net loss of $42.6 million for the six months ended June 30, 2026, compared with a $22.8 million loss during the corresponding period last year.
Windward generated no revenue in either period as it continued investing in clinical development.
The biotechnology firm has raised approximately $365 million in equity financing, including a $165 million funding round completed in May.
That financing was led by OrbiMed Advisors, with participation from Novo Holdings and Omega Fund Management.
Novo Holdings, which manages assets belonging to the Novo Nordisk Foundation, is among Windward’s largest shareholders.
Other major investors include SR One Capital Management, RTW Investments, funds managed by Blue Owl Capital (NYSE), and Chief Executive Luca Santarelli.
Santarelli previously founded and led VectivBio, a gastrointestinal drug developer acquired by Ironwood Pharmaceuticals (NASDAQ) for approximately $1 billion in 2023.
The planned offering is being managed by Jefferies Financial Group (NYSE), Toronto-Dominion Bank (NYSE), Piper Sandler (NYSE) and UBS Group (NYSE).
The filing did not disclose the number of shares to be offered or the expected pricing range.
Proceeds from the listing would support Windward’s ongoing clinical programmes as it advances its experimental therapies towards potential regulatory approval.

title: France’s luxury stores board up windows ahead of fresh protests
full_text:
By Alessandro Parodi
PARIS, Oct 24 (Reuters) - Luxury boutiques in France boarded up their normally glitzy windows and added guards ahead of fresh protests on Saturday, with some planning to stay closed after rioters looted shops across the country last weekend.
France, the most visited country in the world, draws large numbers of overseas shoppers seeking Chanel handbags and Hermes scarves, an important source of revenue for brands facing slowing demand.
But some decided staying open was too risky after last week’s events, when rioters smashed and looted hundreds of shops in Paris, Marseille and Bordeaux.
A Rolex retailer and a De Beers store near the capital’s famous Place Vendome will remain closed on Saturday, staff said, while managers at stores including Richemont-owned IWC said they would decide whether to close early depending on the intensity of the protests.
Groups including France’s main student union UNEF and the Yellow Vest group, which emerged as a potent anti-establishment movement in 2018, plan to march through central Paris later on Saturday to protest against high living costs and cuts to public services.
NOT IN THE MOOD
Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said on Friday that his ministry would deploy 70,000 police officers, backed by specialist units, to prevent the violence that occurred last week.
But staff at LVMH brands Louis Vuitton, Dior and Bulgari said they weren’t taking any chances and security at their stores near Place Vendome had been increased for the day. Additional private security to supplement the police presence in the neighbourhood is also planned.
Nearby department store Printemps also increased its security staff, carried out safety repairs and added security measures to reinforce shop windows and entrances, a spokesperson for the store said.
Hermes finance chief Eric du Halgouet said this week the company had increased security measures at its French stores, adding it was too early to say how much impact recent events would have on business.
The image-conscious industry can ill afford further negative publicity. Consumer sentiment is gloomy worldwide and tourism is slowing as a result of the Iran war — contributing to disappointing quarterly reports at LVMH, Hermes and Kering this month.
Lidiya Shevchenko, a sales assistant at a Graziella Braccialini store, said she doubted many people would be looking to visit stores anyway during the protests.
"I suppose the mood is just as important when it comes to shopping," Shevchenko said.
One tourist who has already been put off is Cambodian Jerry Lay, who purchased several items from Louis Vuitton on the Champs-Élysées earlier this week.
"We do enjoy shopping in France, but after experiencing the protest (last Saturday), I’d say it’s 50/50 whether I would consider coming back next time," Lay said.

title: How agentic AI is reshaping software development
full_text:
Investing.com -- Agentic artificial intelligence is transforming software development, but fears that it will make traditional software companies obsolete are overstated, according to Bank of America analysts.
In a research note, BofA said advances in AI models and autonomous coding tools have reduced software prototyping costs, fuelling concerns about the commoditisation of software development.
However, analysts argued that building functional demonstrations differs significantly from deploying enterprise applications capable of operating securely and reliably at scale.
Challenges involving integration, cybersecurity, maintenance and reliability continue to support demand for established software providers.
The bank expects AI to reshape competitive advantages rather than eliminate them.
Traditional differentiators such as user interfaces, user experience and standardised implementation services could become less valuable as AI automates increasingly complex development tasks.
Conversely, proprietary data, industry expertise, customer relationships and control over AI-driven workflows could become more important competitive advantages.
Software companies operating critical systems of record may also benefit as autonomous agents increasingly depend on trusted business data and established processes.
Pricing remains uncertain, with vendors exploring alternatives to traditional per-user subscriptions, including consumption-based and outcome-based models.
Higher AI inference costs could pressure profitability as companies determine how much customers will pay for automated services.
Despite potential disruption to IT budgets, enterprise software spending is projected to grow approximately 13% annually between 2025 and 2030.
Meanwhile, AI-related revenue disclosures remain inconsistent, with U.S. software companies generally providing more detailed information than European counterparts.
Available disclosures indicate AI contributes approximately 1% to 11% of total company revenue, although BofA believes actual contributions may be understated because AI functionality is frequently bundled into existing products.
Among companies providing medium-term projections, AI revenue is expected to account for roughly 5% to 30% of overall sales.
However, relatively few vendors have published specific monetisation targets, limiting investors’ visibility into the technology’s longer-term financial contribution.

title: UK budget to prioritise bond markets as Labour tensions mount, Bloomberg reports
full_text:
Investing.com -- British Chancellor John Healey is preparing a cautious budget aimed at reassuring bond investors, potentially disappointing Labour lawmakers seeking more ambitious economic reforms under Prime Minister Andy Burnham, Bloomberg reported on Saturday.
Healey’s first budget, scheduled for Wednesday, is expected to prioritise fiscal discipline, avoid broad tax increases and preserve confidence in British government debt.
According to Bloomberg, the Treasury is considering higher taxes on banks to finance targeted, temporary assistance for households struggling with rising energy costs.
The chancellor is also expected to maintain a fiscal buffer of at least £15 billion ($20 billion), based on a Bloomberg survey of primary dealers.
British government bonds have recently outperformed some European peers as investors welcomed signals that the administration would avoid significant increases in borrowing.
However, the approach risks creating tensions within Labour, where lawmakers had anticipated more substantial policy changes following Burnham’s replacement of Keir Starmer in July.
Burnham previously outlined proposals to revise Britain’s Brexit arrangements and establish a national social care service, but the upcoming budget is unlikely to advance those priorities significantly.
Major decisions involving defence expenditure and welfare reductions have also been postponed, according to the report.
Government officials are particularly concerned about the economic consequences of further escalation in the U.S.-Iran conflict, which could disrupt energy supplies and undermine fiscal forecasts.
Treasury officials rejected suggestions that the budget would lack ambition, indicating that additional cost-of-living measures could still be announced.
Some Labour lawmakers have nevertheless expressed frustration that fiscal caution appears to be taking precedence over the government’s broader economic agenda.
The political challenge comes despite improved polling for Labour since Burnham became prime minister, with the party moving ahead of Reform UK.
Meanwhile, disagreements over immigration, welfare reform and the government’s forthcoming 10-year policy plan could further test Labour unity after Wednesday’s budget.

title: Analysis-Trump foreign policy hits voters in the pocketbook, imperiling Republicans in midterms
full_text:
Buy pullback in this chip stock, Mizuho says
By Matt Spetalnick
WASHINGTON, Oct 24 (Reuters) - Foreign policy is rarely the deciding factor in US midterm elections, when economic considerations usually drive voters’ choices.
But this time, with Donald Trump’s war against Iran and his sweeping tariff campaign pushing up costs for Americans, a president’s approach to world affairs has itself become a pocketbook issue.
As the November 3 elections approach, there are growing signs that voters are drawing that connection directly, creating a major liability for Trump and his fellow Republicans and imperiling their control of Congress.
Those include a Reuters/Ipsos poll earlier this month showing some 78% of Americans blame Trump’s policies for rising prices that are outpacing their earnings.
Not since 2006, when President George W. Bush’s Republicans lost both legislative chambers while he was mired in the unpopular Iraq war, has a US leader’s handling of international events appeared so central to shaping the midterms outcome.
The political backlash for Trump could be even bigger, with opinion polls showing that voters feel the economic pain from high gas prices and rising grocery bills in a way that they didn’t two decades ago.
“The bottom line is people are experiencing the impact of Trump’s war and other policies,” said Christopher Preble, a senior fellow at the Stimson Center think tank in Washington. “Now voters have a chance to register their discontent with how he’s dealing with all this.”
POLITICS DRIVING FOREIGN POLICY
With Trump’s approval ratings touching historic lows, he has left little doubt, despite his public claims to the contrary, that he sees the straight line voters are drawing between his foreign policy and their cost of living.
That has prompted some controversial policy moves in the run-up to the elections.
Chief among them was Trump’s lifting of sanctions on Russian diesel exports aimed at bringing down fuel prices, a step his critics, including some fellow Republicans, say reinforces the impression that he is increasingly siding with Moscow in its war in Ukraine.
He has also pressed Kyiv to halt strikes on Russian refineries as he tries to shift the blame for high US gasoline prices despite experts saying the surge in energy costs is mainly the result of the war he launched alongside Israel against Iran nearly eight months ago.
At the same time, he has promised not to order any new attack on Iran before the midterms, though the US and Israel are widely reported to be preparing for a possible major escalation after the elections.
Polls have shown that most voters oppose the war initiated by Trump, who had campaigned on avoiding new foreign interventions. He has insisted Americans should accept temporarily higher gas prices so that he can block Iran from developing a nuclear weapon.
Iran says its nuclear program is for civilian purposes. The UN nuclear watchdog and US intelligence community have assessed that Tehran shuttered a nuclear weapons development program in 2003.
Some Republican candidates have distanced themselves from Trump on matters ranging from the conflict in the Middle East to the trade war with Canada and his pressure campaign against Ukraine.
For its part, Iran has sought to keep oil prices high and hurt Trump in the midterms by deploying new tactics to target ships transiting the Strait of Hormuz and deliberately prolonging the diplomatic stalemate, senior Iranian officials have told Reuters.
Defending the administration’s approach, White House spokesman Matt Middleton said: "President Trump has always been clear about temporary market disruptions as a result of the conflict in Iran, but the contrast between President Trump’s economic record and Democrats’ ruinous alternative is clear."
‘IT’S THE ECONOMY, STUPID’
Midterm elections historically have been seen as a referendum on the performance of the incumbent in the White House.
And in one election after another in recent decades, the conventional wisdom has been that economic concerns - “it’s the economy, stupid,” as the Clinton-era adage goes - dominate voters’ choices.
Opinion polls for this year’s midterms, including the Reuters/Ipsos survey, show that while voters rank foreign policy low on their list of priorities, it is clear that most Americans see some of Trump’s signature moves on the world stage, such as the Iran war and tariffs, feeding into their higher costs.
Other polls have shown that a majority of Americans have also soured more broadly on Trump’s international approach.
The Chicago Council on Global Affairs said its latest nationwide survey “finds that most Americans believe the Trump administration’s foreign policy actions have negatively impacted America’s global standing and hurt national and household economic conditions.”
Since returning to the White House last year, Trump has shaken up the rules-based global order that Washington helped create from the ashes of World War Two while his relations with allies have steadily worsened and the limits of US power have been increasingly exposed, analysts say.
LEGISLATIVE BALANCE OF POWER IN PLAY
Against this backdrop, Democrats are widely projected to gain control of the House of Representatives in the midterms, with the Senate also seen as increasingly in play.
For Republicans, losing either chamber could complicate Trump’s agenda in the last two years of his second term.
But even with a shift in the balance of power on Capitol Hill on November 3, lawmakers will have a hard time reining in Trump’s capacity to pursue foreign policy as he sees fit.
Once the ballots are counted, a big question will be whether Trump will feel either restricted or emboldened on the world stage as he enters what is traditionally considered a lame-duck phase - when a president is barred from running again and no longer faces electoral consequences for decisions made.
“For many presidents who feel politically constrained (at home), foreign policy is the area where they are able to act with relative freedom,” said Jon Alterman of the Center for Strategic and International Studies think tank in Washington.
Analysts say Trump’s handling of adversaries such as Iran, Russia, China and even Cuba or his approach to allies across the globe could go either way -- or he could simply lose interest and double down on his string of construction projects, such as the White House ballroom.

title: UK unveils $800 million AI security funding plan
full_text:
Investing.com -- The British government announced approximately £600 million ($800 million) in artificial intelligence funding on Saturday, targeting biological threats, cybersecurity and critical infrastructure protection.
The largest portion of the funding will support a new biosecurity initiative designed to strengthen Britain’s ability to identify and respond to emerging biological threats.
The programme includes £100 million for an AI-powered laboratory focused on detecting biological threats and another £65 million to develop countermeasures against dangerous pathogens.
AI minister Kanishka Narayan said the government wants the AI Biosecurity Lab to become a leading international institution combining scientific expertise with advanced technology to protect public health.
OpenAI and Anthropic will contribute up to £200 million in AI model credits to support the initiative, while Google DeepMind and London-based biotechnology startup Basecamp Research will provide additional assistance.
The government will also allocate another £120 million to its existing AI Security Institute, strengthening research into the risks posed by increasingly capable AI systems.
Separately, £130 million will fund two cybersecurity initiatives aimed at improving protection across critical infrastructure and the wider economy.
These include the National Cyber Shield and the National Exposure and Real-Time Vulnerability Centre, which will focus on identifying and addressing security vulnerabilities.
Another £60 million will support investments in British companies developing AI applications for robotics, autonomous systems and manufacturing.
The government has earmarked a further £60 million for AI research and procurement contracts, alongside £23 million to examine the technology’s economic impact.
Additional allocations include £18 million for a chip design academy and £15 million for a competition supporting AI solutions to public policy challenges, initially focusing on healthcare.
Regional mayors will receive £30 million to support local AI initiatives, while Britain’s National Cyber Security Centre will receive additional, unspecified funding to expand its Manchester operations.
The announcement comes as AI companies face substantial development costs, with Anthropic alone recording more than $12 billion in operating expenses last year, according to Reuters.

title: Moonshot curbs hacking ability in new Kimi model as fears grow over AI-powered cyberattacks
full_text:
Buy pullback in this chip stock, Mizuho says
By Eduardo Baptista
BEIJING, Oct 24 (Reuters) - Moonshot AI has reduced the cyber-offensive capabilities of its newest model, the Chinese startup said on Saturday, as fears grow that increasingly autonomous AI could turbocharge hacking.
Beijing-based Moonshot announced the curbs while introducing Kimi K3.1 Pro, which it describes as its most capable 3-trillion-parameter-class open-weight model. The company plans to publish the model’s weights — files allowing outside developers to run and modify it on their own systems — by November 4.
Moonshot said it removed cyber-related data from the training corpus and reinforcement-learning environments used to develop the model, while retaining general coding skills.
"We aim not to release open weights that would extend the absolute frontier of cyber capability," the company said.
Governments, technology companies and security researchers are growing increasingly concerned that AI could make sophisticated hacking easier and cheaper. Models that can write code, operate software tools and complete long, multi-step tasks may help users identify weaknesses in programs and automate parts of cyberattacks.
China proposed export controls last week that would ban exports of AI-driven malware-generation and mutation technology and restrict AI-assisted vulnerability-discovery tools. The draft measures, which remain open for public comment, cite the risk that such capabilities could be used against critical infrastructure, defence-industrial and core government systems, or to bypass security protections.
Moonshot said open-weight models can improve security by helping more organisations inspect and secure their own software, including older systems that receive little attention.
Unlike proprietary, closed-weight AI systems, however, open-weight releases make central oversight more difficult. Once the files are widely distributed, the original developer has less ability to restrict access, monitor use or update safeguards than with a hosted service.
K3.1 Pro scored 81.0% on its internal cyber benchmark, compared with 90.5% for a similar version without the risk-reduction measures, the company said. The test involved finding and exploiting software vulnerabilities in a controlled environment. Moonshot said the comparison showed that filtering cyber-related data reduced the model’s offensive cyber performance, although it still outperformed its predecessor. The results have not been independently verified.
K3.1 Pro has a 1-million-token context window, allowing it to process very large amounts of text at once. Moonshot also released a faster version, K3.1 Pro Highspeed, which it said runs at two to three times the speed of the standard model.
